title: TAO-Attack: Toward Advanced Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attacks for Large Language Models
claim: Existing attacks either trigger refusals or yield pseudo-harmful outputs; our two-stage loss suppresses both to produce truly harmful completions.
layout: 3 panels: two stacked prior-method boxes left, tall two-stage ours right; shared prompt banner on top
description: A wide banner at the top holds a malicious question plus a suffix, marked with a devil icon. Below it are two stacked panels on the left, GCG & MAC and I-GCG. On the right is one tall panel for TAO-Attack (Ours), titled in red. Each panel repeats the same pattern: a gray box with the optimization goal, a brain 'LLMs' icon, and a response box. Red and blue arrows show which text is pushed up or down. GCG & MAC ends in a blue 'Refusal' label. I-GCG ends in an orange 'Pseudo-harmful' label with a halo emoji. The TAO panel is split into Stage 1 (refusal-aware loss) and Stage 2 (effectiveness-aware loss). It ends in a red 'Harmful' devil label with real exploit code. Color-coded text carries most of the meaning.
caption: Comparison of optimization-based jailbreak attacks. GCG and MAC can result in refusals, while I-GCG reduces refusals but produces pseudo-harmful outputs. Our TAO-Attack employs a two-stage loss to suppress refusals and penalize pseudo-harmful outputs, leading to more effective harmful completions.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across diverse applications but remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where attackers craft prompts that bypass safety alignment and elicit unsafe responses. Among existing approaches, optimization-based attacks have shown strong effectiveness, yet current methods often suffer from frequent refusals, pseudo-harmful outputs, and inefficient token-level updates. In this work, we propose TAO-Attack, a new optimization-based jailbreak method. TAO-Attack employs a two-stage loss function: the first stage suppresses refusals to ensure the model continues harmful prefixes, while the second stage penalizes pseudo-harmful outputs and encourages the model toward more harmful completions. In addition, we design a direction-priority token optimization (DPTO) strategy that improves efficiency by aligning candidates with the gradient direction before considering update magnitude. Extensive experiments on multiple LLMs demonstrate that TAO-Attack consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving higher attack success rates and even reaching 100\% in certain scenarios.
